key_finding: Across six agents on BrowseComp-Plus and BrowseComp, answer accuracy tracks cumulative retrieval recall far more than the number of searches or context consumed, and the best agents issue far fewer redundant reformulations.
methodology: Trajectory-level diagnosis using human-annotated document relevance judgments, holding the retrieval model fixed while comparing six long-horizon search agents.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's question 2 and undercuts the premise that more agentic search effort is what carries the gain — useful evidence often appears early and agents overshoot, which redirects design attention from 'more iteration' to stopping criteria and evidence selection.
limitations: evaluates existing agents rather than proposing a new system
findings tied to BrowseComp-Plus/BrowseComp corpora, not literature-specific benchmarks
relevance_reason: Decomposes what part of agentic search effort actually produces gains, the exact mechanism-attribution question the brief prioritizes.

key_finding: PaSa-7B beats the best Google+GPT-4o baseline by 37.78% in recall@20 and 39.90% in recall@50 on RealScholarQuery, and exceeds prompted PaSa-GPT-4o by 30.36% recall and 4.25% precision.
methodology: RL-trained LLM agent that invokes search tools, reads papers, and selects references; trained on synthetic AutoScholarQuery (35k queries) and evaluated on a new RealScholarQuery benchmark.
why_it_matters: Gives concrete, large recall gaps over single-query search-engine baselines (Google, Google Scholar) for the exact academic-paper-search task the brief is scanning, anchoring question 1 and offering a benchmark-construction template for question 3.
limitations: trained on synthetic queries derived from top-tier AI conference papers, may not generalize across fields
recall gains not decomposed by which agentic move (search vs. reading vs. citation-following) drives them
relevance_reason: Foundational agentic academic-paper-search system with explicit baseline comparison and benchmark construction, core to the brief's setting.

key_finding: A bounded pipeline of one seed search, 1.5-hop citation expansion, entailment-based pruning, and recency-aware random-walk ranking outperforms proprietary deep-research agents by up to 3x recall@50 at roughly a third of the cost on LitSearch.
methodology: System design paper evaluated on LitSearch and one further benchmark over a 500K-paper arXiv corpus; compares against open-ended deep-research agents built on proprietary LLMs.
why_it_matters: Isolates citation-graph traversal and pruning as the specific mechanisms carrying the gain over open-ended agentic search, directly answering the brief's question 2 with an inspectable, bounded design.
limitations: corpus limited to arXiv (500K papers)
benchmark construction for the 'one further benchmark' not detailed in the abstract
relevance_reason: A structurally-bounded alternative to open-loop deep research agents that explicitly attributes gains to citation-graph traversal, exactly the mechanism decomposition the brief wants.

key_finding: Overlap between human-selected and mid-2025 LLM-selected references across eight expert physics/astrophysics/cosmology projects is under 6%, with 3% fabricated references and 64% carrying at least one incorrect metadata field, though a 2026 model showed zero errors on one test project.
methodology: Controlled parallel comparison of human experts vs. LLM systems (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT Deep Research, Gemini) performing identical literature-review tasks on eight defined research projects.
why_it_matters: Directly tests and largely rejects the brief's premise that agentic literature search reliably matches expert search, giving a concrete low-overlap number to anchor question 1 and a hallucination rate that qualifies any reported agentic gain.
limitations: only eight projects, all in physics/astrophysics/cosmology
improved 2026 model result is a single-project anecdote, not systematically tested
relevance_reason: The sharpest available evidence that current agentic literature search does not reproduce expert recall, which is exactly the hardest-case evidence the brief asks the scan to surface.

key_finding: WisPaper's Deep Search module achieves 22.26% recall on TaxoBench versus 20.92% for an O3 baseline, with its validation model reaching 93.70% accuracy at mitigating retrieval hallucinations.
methodology: Description of an integrated agent system (Scholar Search, Library, AI Feeds) with a validating agentic model, evaluated on TaxoBench.
why_it_matters: Shows only a modest ~1.3-point recall gain over a single-model baseline on an academic search benchmark, evidence that agentic gains in this space can be thin rather than dramatic — relevant to question 4's skepticism.
limitations: TaxoBench construction not described in the abstract
gain over baseline is small and mechanism not isolated from the rest of the pipeline
relevance_reason: An end-to-end academic search agent reporting a quantified, modest recall gain over a single baseline in the brief's exact setting.

key_finding: ReBOL, which uses LLM query reformulations to seed a Bayesian-optimization posterior over relevance before iterative LLM scoring, achieves 46.5% vs. 35.0% recall@100 against the best LLM reranker on Robust04.
methodology: Bayesian optimization framework combining LLM query reformulation and batched LLM relevance scoring, evaluated on five BEIR datasets with two LLM backbones.
why_it_matters: A concrete retrieval/reranking mechanism that isolates query reformulation as an input to a downstream optimization loop, useful for the retrieval layer underlying literature-search agents, though its evaluation is on general IR benchmarks rather than scientific literature search.
limitations: evaluated on general BEIR datasets, not a literature-search-specific benchmark
no explicit statement that the technique transfers to academic paper search
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the retrieval/reranking-method criterion with a query-reformulation-driven mechanism, though its setting is general IR rather than scientific literature search.

key_finding: Removing followable hyperlinks and replacing them with equivalent prose roughly doubles search cost per grounded fact at scale, while grounded coverage remains at ceiling in every condition via read-derived re-querying.
methodology: Pre-registered two-arm controlled experiment (linked vs. link-stripped corpora at 50/500/5000 pages) with an Anthropic Claude agent completing documents via search and fetch tools, 99 episodes, fully reproducible offline.
why_it_matters: Quantifies the cost benefit of link/citation-style traversal for an agent versus search alone, a close analogue of citation-graph traversal, though tested on an organizational wiki rather than scientific literature and without a stated transfer claim.
limitations: corpus is a synthetic organizational wiki, not a scientific-literature corpus
unusual venue and no explicit claim the finding transfers to academic citation graphs
relevance_reason: A rigorously controlled test of link/graph-traversal value for agent search cost, close in mechanism to the brief's citation-graph-traversal question but off-domain in setting.

key_finding: LATTICE, an LLM-guided hierarchical search index with no embedding model in the retrieval loop, reaches 46.7 nDCG@10 on BRIGHT (matching the best fine-tuned ensemble) and 49.1 with a lightweight ensemble, while remaining competitive on SciFact and SciDocs.
methodology: Top-down LLM-guided construction of a hierarchical document index from multi-level summaries, plus calibrated path-aggregated LLM traversal at query time; evaluated on BRIGHT, NQ, SciFact, SciDocs.
why_it_matters: Shows the standard embedding-retriever-plus-LLM-verifier pipeline fails when embeddings miss top-k, and offers a retrieval architecture that removes that failure mode — directly relevant to the retrieval/reranking layer underlying literature-search agents, with explicit evaluation on scientific-literature benchmarks (SciFact, SciDocs).
limitations: reasoning-intensive benchmark focus (BRIGHT) is broader than academic paper search specifically
sliding-window reranking beats it at low token budgets, limiting when the advantage holds
relevance_reason: A core retrieval/reranking method directly evaluated on scientific-literature benchmarks, bearing on the brief's retrieval-layer and baseline-ceiling questions.

key_finding: On a fixed, human-verified corpus, Search-R1 with BM25 achieves only 3.86% accuracy versus GPT-5's 55.9%, and pairing GPT-5 with a Qwen3-Embedding-8B retriever raises accuracy to 70.1% with fewer search calls.
methodology: Introduces a fixed-corpus derivative of BrowseComp with human-verified supporting documents and mined hard negatives, enabling controlled disentanglement of agent and retriever contributions.
why_it_matters: The controlled-corpus benchmark other candidates in this scan build directly on (evaluation substrate, projection studies); it sets a concrete, reproducible baseline separating retriever quality from agent reasoning, which the brief's question 1 and 3 both need.
limitations: queries are general knowledge-intensive questions, not academic-paper-finding queries specifically
corpus was assembled per-query from supporting docs plus mined negatives, a construction choice later shown to bias results (see companion projection study)
relevance_reason: The canonical fair/transparent benchmark for deep-research/search agents that underlies several other shortlisted papers' evaluations, central to the brief's benchmark-construction question.

key_finding: Search agents show 'inertia bias' — reduced objectivity when judging outcomes of their own prior actions — and context isolation at webpage triage and answer validation (NIS-Agent) recovers competitive performance while cutting token cost by 33%.
methodology: Introduces the IBIS benchmark controlling search observations to isolate self-authored-action bias, then proposes and evaluates NIS-Agent on GAIA, WebWalkerQA, BrowseComp, BrowseComp-zh.
why_it_matters: Identifies a subtle, previously unattributed failure mode in agentic self-evaluation that degrades search agent performance, relevant to question 4's search for where reported agentic designs underperform expectations.
limitations: benchmarks are general web/QA agents, not literature-search specific
gain is attributed to a bias-correction mechanism rather than the reformulation/graph-traversal/crawling moves the brief names directly
relevance_reason: A mechanism-level failure-mode analysis of deep research agents with a purpose-built benchmark, adjacent to but not centered on the brief's named agentic moves.

key_finding: Structured field extraction in HySemRAG achieves 35.1% higher semantic similarity (0.655 vs 0.485, p<0.000001) than PDF-chunking, with 68.3% single-pass QA success and 99.0% citation accuracy across 643 evaluation observations.
methodology: Hybrid retrieval (semantic search, keyword filtering, knowledge-graph traversal) plus agentic self-correction and citation verification, applied to geospatial epidemiology literature via a Neo4j/Qdrant pipeline.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a concrete hybrid retrieval+graph-traversal architecture with citation verification for literature synthesis, giving a retrieval-method data point for question 3, though its headline metrics are about extraction quality rather than search recall.
limitations: applied to a single domain (ozone/cardiovascular epidemiology) as a case study
does not isolate which of semantic search, keyword filtering, or graph traversal drives the reported gains
relevance_reason: A hybrid retrieval architecture for scientific literature synthesis combining the exact retrieval and graph-traversal components the brief tracks under question 3.

key_finding: A taxonomy of Deep Research agent architectures (static/dynamic workflows, single/multi-agent, API vs. browser retrieval) alongside a critical assessment finding current benchmarks limited by restricted external-knowledge access, sequential-execution inefficiency, and metrics misaligned with agents' practical objectives.
methodology: Narrative systematic review and taxonomy synthesis, no abstract-stated protocol; includes a maintained repository of DR agent research.
why_it_matters: Gives an orienting map of the mechanisms and benchmark weaknesses across the field, directly informing which specific agentic moves and which benchmark flaws the scan should watch for in questions 2 through 4.
limitations: abstract-only, narrative rather than systematic-protocol review
does not itself measure baseline recall or replication failure, only synthesizes others' findings
relevance_reason: The field-level synthesis a research scan needs to place individual system and benchmark papers in context, and the required review-flagged entry.

key_finding: Relocating BrowseComp-Plus's evidence into the independently-built ClimbMix corpus drops the strongest agent's evidence recall from 84.3% to 21.4% and answer accuracy by five points while it issues 63% more search calls, despite the questions being unchanged.
methodology: A projection pipeline that decomposes each question into atomic reasoning hops and re-grounds them in a new 553M-document corpus, retaining only hops verified by automatic checking, an independent agent, and human review; applied to 830 BrowseComp-Plus questions, yielding 57 fully grounded questions.
why_it_matters: Direct, quantified evidence that a reported agentic-search benchmark result is substantially inflated by the original corpus's per-query construction, exactly the question-4 evidence the brief prioritizes finding.
limitations: pipeline yields only 57 grounded questions from 830, a small evaluation set
first of a planned series, so generalization to other benchmarks beyond BrowseComp-Plus is not yet demonstrated
relevance_reason: The clearest available demonstration that an agentic search benchmark's construction inflates reported gains, directly answering the brief's hardest question.

key_finding: PaperPilot-9B, a multi-turn literature-search agent that induces an executable DAG of search operators (keyword search, citation expansion, filtering, scoring, reranking, evidence extraction), raises Hit@5 from 58.0 to 77.0, MRR from 47.5 to 59.4, and nDCG@10 from 26.8 to 32.5 over a base toolset agent, while cutting workflow execution errors from 9.5% to 0%.
methodology: Supervised workflow imitation plus preference optimization over controlled workflow corruptions; evaluated against a Qwen3.5-9B toolset agent baseline under multi-turn interaction. Abstract-only for full experimental detail.
why_it_matters: Directly tests what agentic moves add over an undifferentiated toolset agent by making the workflow explicit and editable — the closest evidence in this shortlist to decision 2 (which specific moves carry the gain), though the baseline compared against is another agent rather than a clean single-query database search ceiling, so it cannot answer decision 1.
limitations: baseline is a toolset agent, not a single-query BM25/embedding/API baseline, so the recall ceiling question (C1) is not addressed
no discussion of how the evaluation query/relevance set was constructed
gains reported on one model family (Qwen3.5-9B) with no cross-benchmark or replication check
relevance_reason: A literature-search agent that explicitly attributes measured gains to named agentic operators (citation expansion, reranking, workflow refinement), squarely in the brief's setting.

key_finding: EviReform, which forms residual queries from retrieved passages to guide graph-based multi-hop retrieval toward evidence left underspecified by the original question, exceeds the strongest baseline by up to 5.59 Recall@5 points and 4.50 F1 points on 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue.
methodology: Retrieval architecture separating query revision from graph-based evidence aggregation, normalizing and combining original and residual retrieval signals, propagated across propositions sharing entities; evaluated on three multi-hop QA benchmarks. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Isolates exactly the kind of mechanism the brief's C2/C3 criteria ask about — query reformulation combined with graph-structured retrieval — with a quantified, ablatable gain, but the evidence is built and evaluated entirely on multi-hop QA retrieval rather than scientific literature search agents, so it can sharpen technique choices without answering the brief's recall-ceiling or benchmark-construction questions in its own setting.
limitations: evaluated on general multi-hop QA datasets, not literature-search corpora or agentic search benchmarks
no discussion of benchmark construction, contamination, or labeling
baseline compared against is the 'strongest baseline' in QA retrieval literature, not a single-query database search ceiling as the brief defines it
relevance_reason: Describes a query-reformulation-plus-graph-retrieval mechanism structurally close to citation-graph traversal, but demonstrated only in multi-hop QA, not literature search — a technique to note, not a direct answer to the brief's questions.
